title: AI customer service: what works, what fails, and how to test it
description: How AI answers customer questions in chat, email and phone, what a federal regulator found about chatbot failures, and how to test one before launch.
summary: AI customer service software answers customer questions in chat, email or by phone and hands the hard cases to a person. It works best on simple, repeated questions and worst on unusual problems.

example.input: A customer writes: I was charged twice for my order last week and I want one charge refunded.
example.output: The AI finds the order, confirms the duplicate charge, explains the refund steps and timing, and passes it to a person if the refund is above your set limit.

howToTest: Pull 200 real past conversations and sort them by type: simple, tricky and angry.
Replay the questions and have your best support agent grade each answer as correct, wrong or incomplete.
Test hand-off. Ask for a person in many ways and confirm the customer reaches one fast.
Try to trick it into a false promise, such as a refund outside your policy, and see if it holds.
After a small live launch, compare resolution rate, repeat contacts and customer ratings against humans only.

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy when you use a standard help desk and want to start with your most common questions in weeks.
buyVsBuild.build: Build when the answers depend on complex internal data or you need strict control over every sentence.

watchOuts: The CFPB's 2023 report found chatbots may be useful for basic inquiries but their effectiveness wanes as problems get more complex.
The same report says companies may be liable for legal violations when a chatbot fails to comply with consumer laws.
Customers stuck in a loop with no human are a real harm. Always offer a person.
A wrong answer stated with confidence is worse than saying it does not know.

sources.name: CFPB: Chatbots in consumer finance (June 2023)
sources.what: Finds chatbots may resolve basic inquiries but are less effective as problems grow more complex, and that institutions risk violating legal obligations and eroding trust. It estimates about 37% of the U.S. population interacted with a bank's chatbot in 2022.

sources.name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
sources.what: Describes the framework, released January 26, 2023, as voluntary and meant to build trustworthiness into AI design, use and evaluation.
